title: How many checks a reading carries
statement: How many comprehension checks a reading should carry is unsettled: too many on a short text may stop learners forming a mental model of it.
example: One course's design documents say exactly 2 comprehension checks per reading, while its shipped lessons ran 4.
detail: A review of a Grade 3 reading unit asked whether it asked so many questions that children missed the point, warning that questions had been overdone on texts too short for the mental model to form. The shipped convention was four comprehension checks per reading against design documents that say exactly two, and the challenge collided with the course's response-rate ceilings and with its rule that every inference point is cashed by a question. It was routed for a ruling that had not come, and a later ruling to lean toward literal checks at first covers only those and does not resolve the overall count.
against: The interim ruling for literal checks leans toward more checks at first: "lean MORE toward sync checks initially, then dial back on reviewer request." (grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g3-reading/iteration-6/distilled/03-INSTRUCTION-DESIGN.md, lines 214-215). The records few-questions-during-reading and hold-a-lessons-load-steady argue for few, budgeted questions.

evidence.quote: We've overdone questions to a detriment that we're not even allowing the mental model to occur. … too much with texts that are too short.
